title: WPMS/1873/2016 of Mahendra Singh Vs M/s Dabar India Ltd

paras.text:
HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Writ Petition (M/S) No. 1873 of 2016
Mahendra Singh ...Petitioner
Vs.
M/s Dabar India Limited ...Respondent
With
Writ Petition (M/S) No. 2071 of 2016
Navin Chandra Pandey ...Petitioner
Vs.
M/s Dabar India Limited, SIDCUL ...Respondent
Advocate: Mr. G.D. Joshi, Advocate for the petitioner
Mr. T.A. Khan, Senior Advocate, assisted by Mr. Ravi Babulkar,
Advocate for the respondent
Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.
(Via Video Conferencing)
These are the two connected writ petitions, which are arising
out of an award, rendered on 19.06.2015. As well as, the challenge is
also given by the petitioners to the order dated 17.12.2015, both
passed by the learned Labour Court, Kashipur, District Udham Singh
Nagar, by virtue of which an application for recall, which was
preferred by the petitioner, seeking to set aside the award has been
rejected.
2. In WPSS No. 1873 of 2016, the aforesaid two orders have
been passed in relation to an Adjudication Case No. 31 of 2011,
Mahendra Singh Vs. Dabar India Limited, SIDCUL, Pant Nagar.
Whereas, in WPSS No. 2071 of 2016, which is the connected writ
petition, the impugned award had been rendered in Adjudication
Case No. 32 of 2011, Navin Chandra Pandey Vs. Dabar India
Limited.
3. Before dealing with the argument as extended by the learned
counsel for the petitioner, it becomes inevitable for this Court to
avoid consideration of the factual backdrops, as involved
consideration in the aforesaid two writ petitions.

2
4. In Writ Petition No 1873 of 2016, Mahendra Singh Vs. Dabar
India Limited, the factual backdrops are that the petitioner, had come
up with the case that after conducting the interview on 23.08.2004,
the petitioner contends that he was appointed with the respondent in
the capacity of 'Chemist Supervisor'. Subsequent thereto, he
contends that owing to the past services rendered by him since being
unblemished, his services stood regularised with the respondent by
an order which was passed in the month of June, 2006. The case of
the petitioner in the writ petition is further that since the
respondent/employer, they were engaging themselves in adopting
measures, which were detriment to the interest of the workmen,
working in the respondent organisation, the petitioner is alleged to
have starting making efforts to get the trade union of the workers
registered with the Registrar of Trade Union and for the said
purpose, this act was not welcomed by the respondent. It is an
allegation of the respondent in the proceedings before the labour
Court that the petitioner, along with the other workers had engaged
themselves in filing of an application before the Registrar, Trade
Union on 25.06.2009, for getting the trade union registered, in order
to protect the workmen working in the production unit of the
respondent employer.
5. The argument of the learned counsel for the petitioner is that
this act of the petitioner of making efforts to get the trade union
registered, in order to protect the interests of the workmen was not
welcomed by the respondent/employer, due to which the
management had orally passed an order dated 14.07.2009, whereby
the entry of the petitioner into the factory premises of the
respondent/employer was prohibited. When the petitioner agitated
his hue and cry, as against the arbitrary act of the respondent by
stopping the entry of the workman petitioner into the premises of the
respondent, the petitioner and such other workmen represented their
grievances before the respondent and five representatives of the so-called proposed trade unions which was expected to be registered
were called to hold a meeting for settlement of the dispute.

3
6. The settlement proceeding, which was thus instituted between
the five representatives of the trade unions and with the
respondent/employer, the proposal and the terms & conditions
offered and extended by the respondent for continuing the services of
the workmen, who were allegedly stopped to enter the premises of
the factory, is that the said proposal since was not conducive to the
expectations of the workman, the workmen declined to accept the
proposal, hence the effort for settlement failed.
7. On account of failure of the meeting, which was held between
them to settle the scores, the case of the petitioner is that further in
order to exert pressure on the employees/workmen because of their
engagement in making efforts to protect the interest of the workers,
working in the factory of the respondent by registering the trade
union, it is alleged that the entire action of the respondent become so
malicious that they had even proceeded to register an FIR against the
workman.
8. The respondent had contended that on account of an attempt
and also because of an act of misbehaviour, at the behest of the
petitioner and his other allies and representatives, the petitioner was
placed under suspension by the respondent by an order dated
15.07.2009 (Annexure 1 to the supplementary counter affidavit of
respondent No. 2). If the order of petitioners' suspension itself is
taken into consideration, the precise set of allegations levelled
against the petitioner was that of an act of misbehaviour with the
security personnel, who were on duty, who had stopped the entry of
the petitioner from a particular gate, which was not available or open
for the workmen to enter the premises as they were suppose to enter
the factory premises from another gate, provided to them.
9. The allegations were, that when the security personnel
obstructed the entry of the petitioner, in the premises of the factory
from the gate from which the workmen cannot enter the premises, it
was not welcomed, it was alleged in the suspension order while
explaining the precise charges that the petitioner had rather

4
misbehaved and used abusive language against the security
personnel, as well as against the members of the management and
created an unruly environment.
10. Despite the request made by the security personnel to the
petitioner to enter the premises from the gates specified for the
workmen, when the petitioner did not agreed with that, it is alleged
in the suspension order that the petitioner entered the factory
premises forcefully from the same gate and by forcefully entering
into the chamber of Assistant Manager (HR), he had misbehaved and
had also used abusive language against the Manager (HR) of the
respondent company.
11. The suspension order further observed, that when the
settlement proceeding, which was being held by way of a meeting,
could not succeed and when the disturbance was created by the
petitioner on 14.07.2009, and their demands were not acceded to by
the management, the workers gave a call for a strike, and on account
of this attitude of rioting against the management and indiscipline,
the respondent contended that the employer has suffered huge
business loss, resulting into the passing of an order of suspension,
contending thereof that the acts complained of in the suspension
order happens to be a misconduct under the certified Standing Orders
as applicable.
12. The petitioner in the writ petition has submitted that the order
of suspension of his services would be unreasonable; for the reason
being that it was without application of mind and that too
particularly when no valid reason was assigned in it and further that
the suspension was without providing an opportunity of hearing to
him.
13. Let this Court, at this stage itself clarify that under the service
jurisprudence wherever the disciplinary rules as applicable to the
service conditions to an employee grants the power of suspension to
an employee on the ground of misconduct, the provision of

5
suspension in itself does not contemplate a prior opportunity of
hearing, prior to suspending an employee. Hence, this ground, at this
stage itself is refused to be accepted as legally not sustainable.
14. On the service of the order of suspension, the petitioner was
called upon to participate in the disciplinary proceedings by
submission of his reply to the chargesheet dated 25.07.2009, which
was submitted against him. But he had refused to submit the reply to
the charges and as a consequence thereto, the departmental enquiry
proceeding which was initiated against him by the appointment of
enquiry officer, who conducted the disciplinary proceedings and
submitted his departmental enquiry report against the petitioner,
holding thereof that prima facie set of allegations levelled against the
petitioner, in the chargesheet, did stood proved against him. On the
contrary, the case of the petitioner is that it is not a correct fact that
he had declined to file the reply to the chargesheet; but rather to the
contrary, he has pleaded in the writ petition that when he attempted
to file his reply to the chargesheet, that was refused to be accepted by
the respondent/employer and an ex parte disciplinary proceeding was
conducted and concluded against him, resulting into submission of
the enquiry report dated 12.02.2010, against the petitioner, which he
contends that would be in absolute violation of principle of natural
justice as it was submitted without providing any opportunity to the
petitioner to cross-examine the witnesses. An additional ground,
which was taken by the petitioner in the writ petition is that much
reliance cannot be placed in the departmental enquiry proceeding
and the report dated 12.02.2010, for the reason being that the enquiry
officer, who was appointed was on the choice of the
respondent/employer that itself would vitiate the conclusion drawn
by the enquiry officer in the enquiry report submitted by him on
12.02.2010.
15. The respondent/employer issued a show cause notice, to the
petitioner, prior to passing of the order of termination, and on the
conclusion of the enquiry, which is a fact, admitted by the petitioner
in para 11 of the writ petition. Petitioner's contention is that without

6
awaiting the reply to be considered, the respondent/employer had, on
account of the fact that when despite of show cause, no reply was
submitted by the petitioner with regard to the charges of misconduct,
which stood proved in the enquiry report dated 12.02.2010, the
respondent had issued a publication in Dainik Jagran Newspaper of
Kumaon Division on 27.02.2010, wherein, by way of a publication,
the respondent/employer had sought an explanation from the
petitioner to the enquiry report and second show cause notice was
issued to the petitioner, prior to imposition of punishment on the
establishment of the charge of misconduct against the petitioner.
16. The order of dispensation of service of the petitioner dated
06.03.2010, records the finding that despite of an opportunity being
granted to the petitioner to represent his case as against the findings
of the enquiry report, and as against the proposed punishment on the
establishment of the charge against him, when despite of show cause
notice dated 25.02.2010, and when despite of publication having
being made on 27.02.2010, when the petitioner had voluntarily not
availed the opportunity to submit his explanation, the
respondent/employer had proceeded to terminate the services of the
petitioner after giving him 30 days' salary to the tune of Rs.
33921.89 which was to be deposited into the bank account of the
petitioner by way of cheque bearing No. 356752 dated 06.03.2010.
The petitioner has contended in his writ petition that this order of
dismissal from the services dated 06.03.2010, in fact, was
communicated to the petitioner at a much belated stage on
11.03.2010. Consequent to it, he admits that he preferred a
departmental appeal as against the dismissal order, which was also
rejected by the appellate authority.
17. The petitioner, for the purposes of redressal of his grievance as
against the dismissal order dated 06.03.2010, had sought the
settlement of dispute by holding a request for a conciliation
proceedings prior to making a reference to the labour court for an
adjudication to be made under Section 4(k) of the U.P. Industrial
Disputes Act of 1947. The conciliation proceedings too failed. Later

7
the State Government, by a Government Order No. 4837/Shram
Sewa/631/2002 dated 24.10.2002, had made the following reference
for an adjudication of dispute, by the labour court, vide its order
dated 07.03.2011, as rendered by the Deputy Labour Commissioner.
The reference thus determined to be made was to the following
effect:
In Writ Petition No. 1873 of 2016 (Adjudication Case No. 31 of
2011)

18. On registration of the reference, an Adjudication Case No. 31
of 2011 was registered in the matters of petitioner of WPSS No.
1873 of 2016 and an Adjudication Case No. 32 of 2011 was
registered in the matters of petitioner of WPSS No. 2071 of 2016.
19. Before the labour court, the petitioner has filed his written
statement on 02.09.2011, contending thereof that the entire action
taken against them by the employer culminating to the dismissal
from services on 06.03.2010, is absolutely arbitrary and malicious
because the entire proceeding which has been initiated and later held
as a consequence of suspension from services on 15.07.2009, vitiates
the terms and conditions of the standing orders and happens to be in
utter violation of principle of natural justice. The petitioner further
attributed that the disciplinary proceeding itself was defective,
because he was not provided adequate and an effective opportunity
to defend himself hence the dismissal order from the services would
be vitiated and sought that the reference as was made on 07.03.2011,
may be answered in his favour.

8
20. The respondent/employer filed their written statement and in
response thereto, the petitioner has filed his replication, to the written
statement of the employer on 24.12.2011. On the exchange the
pleadings, the proceeding of respective Adjudication Cases started.
21. Primarily, the workman/petitioner had submitted before the
labour Court that the entire disciplinary proceedings were vitiated
because he was not provided with an adequate and reasonable
opportunity to lead evidence, though this fact was denied in the
proceedings before the labour court by the respondent/employer on
the ground that in the disciplinary proceedings, the petitioner was
given an ample of opportunity to defend himself, but he himself has
rather not availed it and hence he cannot now have a case, that he
was not provided with an effective opportunity of hearing.
22. The facts, which could be borne out from the records are that
when the enquiry officer, initiated the proceedings, he by virtue of an
order date 22.08.2009, has sent a communication to the petitioner,
fixing 01.09.2009, as a date fixed for conducting the domestic
enquiry, but the petitioner himself had not appeared on the said date.
Consequently, the enquiry officer had yet again fixed 02.09.2009, as
the next date fixed. Petitioner participated in the proceeding which
were held on 07.09.2009, and for the first time made a denial to the
charges referred in the chargesheet dated 25.07.2009, on the pretext
that it has not been served upon him hence he was incapacitated to
submit his reply to the charges levelled against him.
23. In order to overcome the said objection as was raised by the
petitioner, the enquiry officer supplied him the copy of the
chargesheet and thereafter the petitioner also participated in the
domestic enquiry which was held on 10.09.2009 and had filed his
reply. Rather he has also appointed his authorised representatives as
representing officer of his case i.e. Kailash Khulbe, who placed his
case as defence representative but on the date fixed when the
proceeding was being taken, the petitioner has not appeared till
24.09.2009, which was the date fixed.

9
24. When petitioner appeared and had raised his objection, the
records showed that it was disposed of by the enquiry officer by
suitably answering all the objections taken by the petitioner. The
records further show that subsequent thereto on 07.10.2009 and
13.10.2009, which were the date fixed, the petitioner had
participated only on one of the dates of the proceedings i.e. on
13.10.2009, and submitted his objection as against the appointment
of the presenting officer. While dealing with the pleadings, the
finding has been recorded by the labour court that as per the record
which has been produced before it, the statement was recorded of
one of the witnesses Mr. Avnesh Yadav on 13.10.2009, and
thereafter 29.10.2009 was the next date fixed for continuing the
proceedings, but the petitioner once again had absented himself from
participating in the enquiry proceedings and on his own choice, he
has presented himself in the enquiry thereafter only on 06.11.2009,
but later on, on that date of the proceeding as fixed by the authorities
he had voluntarily abandoned the disciplinary proceedings even
without signing the attendance register to record and show his
presence in the enquiry proceedings.
25. On account of this attitude and aptitude of the petitioner, the
enquiry officer was constrained to fix 24.11.2009 and 25.11.2009,
for further conducting the disciplinary proceeding but the petitioner
had voluntarily not presented himself. Owing to this aptitude of the
petitioner of not presenting himself before the enquiry officer for
recording his statement, according to his choice, it was not
welcomed and otherwise also too it was contrary to the procedures
contemplated under the standing orders of the government as
notified regulating the procedure for conducting the disciplinary
proceedings. The enquiry officer by an order dated 26.11.2009 had
closed the evidence of the respondent/employer and had recorded a
finding in his report to the effect that as against the oral witnesses
which were adduced by the respondent/employer, the petitioner had
voluntarily not cross-examined their witnesses. In the absence of
non-cross examination of the witnesses, which were adduced by the

10
respondent/employer, the enquiry officer precautionarily vide his
communication dated 12.12.2009, supplied the copies of the
statement of the witnesses recorded on behalf of the
respondent/employer to the petitioners and in order to provide him a
last opportunity, the enquiry officer once again had sent an
information to the petitioner to re-participate in the enquiry, which
was fixed for 26.12.2009. The petitioner did not appear.
Consequently, the enquiry officer submitted his report, resulting into
passing of the order of termination dated 06.03.2010.
26. These facts have been narrated by this Court, though was not
necessary, but with the particular purpose for the reason being that
the petitioner had come up with the case in the writ petition, that the
learned labour court has not provided him an opportunity of hearing;
when the labour court was ceased with deciding the reference and
particularly in the context of the reason for the absence of availing
the opportunity, as argued by the counsel for the petitioner, it was on
the ground that the counsel, whom he had engaged to present the
case before the labour court, had not presented himself on the date
fixed and hence the petitioner cannot be made responsible to suffer
for any of the flaws which has been conduced due to non-participation in the proceedings before the labour court by his
counsel as he cannot be held responsible and made to suffer due to
mistake committed by his counsel.
27. This argument; of the learned counsel for the petitioner of
attributing the responsibility of absence before the labour court on
his counsel, cannot be accepted by this Court for the reason being
that :-
(i) It is not a ground, which is put to challenge in the present writ
petition, while assailing the award of labour court as it is not
pleaded.
(ii) There is nothing on record which was brought by the
petitioner at any stage of the proceedings that the petitioner had
taken any action against the so-called counsel, who had not appeared

11
on his behalf before the labour court after his engagement by the
petitioner, to represent his case as a professional.
(iii) When agent appointed by the petitioner to represent his case
had voluntarily not appeared, it would amount to be an absence of
the principal i.e. petitioner himself, who was represented in the
proceedings before labour Court through his agent and later on an
award being rendered against him, he cannot contend that he was not
heard by the labour court.
(iv) This Court has deliberately considered the past conduct of the
petitioner, which was apparent during the departmental proceedings
with regard to diligence with which he has represented himself
before the enquiry officer prior to passing of the order of dismissal,
which shows the mental inclination of the petitioner and his
negligent attitude towards the proceedings.
28. In order to elucidate the conduct of the petitioner in the
proceedings which were held before the labour court, where he
himself once again has not participated in it. Even if the order sheet
of the proceedings before the labour court, which has been annexed
with the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner dated
12.08.2020, is taken into consideration, which rather reflects the
conduct of the petitioner, as on most of the dates, the petitioner had
deliberately avoided to participate in the proceedings and had been
consistently seeking adjournments before the labour court.
29. In the proceedings, which are held before any court of law,
once it had procedurally issued notices to an adversary to the
proceedings before it to participate in it, if the opposite party on
his/her wisdom chooses not to appear, the labour court or fact that
matter any other Court also has got no other option but except to
proceed in the absence, and the said fact about the diligence with
which the petitioner had participated in the proceedings is quite
apparent from the order sheet which has been recorded by the labour
court annexed as CA4 to the counter affidavit.

12
30. Owing to the aforesaid conduct of the petitioner, the labour
court was constrained to pass the order dated 26.03.2015, in the
reference proceedings, which was initiated to be adjudicated on
07.03.2011, whereby the opportunity to lead evidence of the
petitioner, was closed and the matter was directed to proceed against
the petitioner.
31. The conduct and diligence of the petitioner could very well be
reflected from CA4, wherein the labour court has recorded a finding
that despite of there being several opportunities granted to the
petitioner to lead his evidence, to record his statements, but he has
never availed it, consequently the labour court had to pass an order
on 26.03.2015, closing his opportunity of leading evidence.
32. The order sheet further shows that though the opportunity to
lead the evidence of the petitioner, was closed by an order dated
26.03.2015, he is shown to have filed an application for recall of the
order being paper No. 47d, on which the time was sought by the
respondent/employer to file their objection. Time was granted by the
labour Court to the respondent and 07.05.2015 was the date fixed.
The labour Court on the said recall application, directed the
representative of the petitioner to ask the petitioner to appear and
participate in the proceedings, which was fixed for 04.06.2015. The
order sheet of 04.06.2015, yet again remarks that the petitioner did
not participate in the proceedings nor any evidence was laid by him
nor he has filed any adjournment application requesting for some
other date.
33. Owing to the aforesaid circumstances, the labour court on
19.06.2015, passed an award and answered the reference, against the
petitioner. The labour court observed that if the entire proceedings
which have been initiated against the petitioner right from the date of
suspension i.e. dated 15.07.2009 till 04.06.2015, is taken into
consideration, the petitioner, despite having been provided with
several and ample of opportunities to lead his evidence has not
availed it. But since he has not availed those opportunities, the

13
labour court vide its award dated 19.06.2015, declined to answer the
reference in favour of the petitioner by making the following
observations: -

34. The petitioner contending thereof that the award dated
19.06.2015 happens to be ex parte had filed an application for
recalling of the award by way of Miscellaneous Case which has been
registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 48 of 2015 and the said
Miscellaneous Case too was rejected by one of the impugned
judgement under challenge herein i.e. dated 17.12.2015.
35. The labour court, while considering the application for recall
had recorded the finding that the petitioner had voluntarily derelicted
himself by not diligently participating in the proceedings. The reason
given by the petitioner that his allegation that his representative had
not appeared cannot be taken as to be a rescue or an excuse for the
reason that in the light of the provisions contained under Rule 32 of
the U.P. Labour Court and Labour Tribunal Rules 1967. As far as the
findings, which have been recorded by the labour Court while
rejecting the application for recall are that the petitioner had on his
choice absented himself on 15.01.2015 and has sought for an
adjournment, after granting it the court fixed 25.02.2015, he and his
representative absented themselves on that day too, thereafter the
court fixed 26.03.2015, still on the said date also none of them
appeared thus the Court had no option except to record its finding
with regard to the deliberate act of non appearance despite of the fact
that the petitioner had been noticed to the proceedings consequently
the recall was rejected.

14
36. In support of his contention, the learned counsel for the
petitioner submits that in view of the ratio laid down by the various
pronouncements rendered by the Court; from the view point that for
the cause of a mistake committed by the counsel representing the
cause of the litigant, a litigant may not be made to suffer. There
cannot be any doubt on this proposition, that for the mistake of a
counsel, the litigant should not suffer. But if this proposition, if it is
dealt with in a different prospective and a situation where the
counsel, who has been engaged by a party to the proceedings, if he
does not strategically participate or if he participates in the
proceedings before the Courts with lack of diligence, whether it
could still itself vitiate the proceedings or not. The said principle
cannot be made as a universal principle, the wider principles of the
judgement of the Hon'ble Apex Court, on which reliance has been
placed by the petitioner as reported in AIR 1981, SC 1400, Rafiq and
Another Vs. Munshilal and Another, the reliance placed by the
petitioner is to para 2 of the said authority, which reads as follows:
"2. We have heard Mr. O. P. Rana, learned Counsel for the
appellant, and Mr. A.K. Sanghi, learned Counsel for the
respondent. The High Court disposed of the appeal preferred
by the present appellant in the absence of the learned
Counsel for the appellant. When the appellant became aware
of the fact that his appeal had been disposed of in the
absence of his advocate, he moved an application in the
High Court to recall the order dismissing his appeal and
permit him to participate in the hearing of the appeal. This
application was rejected by the High Court on the ground
that though the application was prepared and drafted and an
affidavit was sworn on 29th October, 1980, the same was
not presented to the court till November 12, 1980 and that
there is no satisfactory explanation for this slackness on the
part of the learned advocate who was requested to file the
application."
37. What is important herein is that the said judgement was in
light of altogether a different perspective and under an entirely
different context, where on account of the personal reasons of the
counsel, the case was dismissed for want of prosecution and the
slackness, which was mentioned and dealt therein was the inability
on part of the advocate to file the affidavit within the time specified.
In the instant case, it is not the case, where the matter was dismissed
in default or for want of prosecution, but rather it was a case where

15
the counsel has not presented himself to argue the matter on several
occasions, when the case was heard by the labour court. Such an
absence, particularly before a labour Court proceedings cannot be
ignored, and that too particularly when the party to the proceedings
or their counsel does not recurring by appear to assist the court, to
arrive to a logical conclusion and hence reasons which have been
assigned that the petitioner has not availed the opportunity to lead his
case would be absolutely unjustified because Courts are not
supposed to solicit the presence of the advocate, engaged by party to
the proceedings rather it is the professional duty of the counsel to
appear and if he does not appear then that cannot be taken as a
latitude to recall the application.
38. Another judgement, on which the reliance has been placed by
the learned counsel for the petitioner, is that reported in 1996 ACJ
516, Qaiser Sibtain Vs. District Judge, Allahabad wherein the
coordinate Bench of Allahabad High Court has held that the conduct
of the litigant and the diligence of his in participating the
proceedings held prior to the consideration of a particular application
for restoration; is not to be taken into consideration. The said
judgement has postulated that a particular application itself has to be
considered exclusively on its own merits and not on the basis of the
previous conduct of absence, cannot be taken for the purposes of
deciding an application.
39. This is factually not the case involved here. The fact of
absence of the counsel in the proceedings has been established. The
past conduct of not participating in the disciplinary proceedings was
not attributed to the counsel, but rather to the petitioner himself, who
has knowingly had not effectively participated in the disciplinary
proceedings resulting into passing of the impugned order of
dispensation of his services. Hence, the circumstances which has
been dealt with by the said judgement is entirely under different
circumstances as that which is prevailing in the present case, because
the petitioner himself has not participated in the proceedings with
diligence when the matter was taken up before the labour Court.

16
40. The petitioner has placed reliance yet upon an another
judgement rendered by the coordinate Bench of this Court, reported
in 2014 Supreme UK 2373, (also reported in 2014 (1) UD 373,
Prem Ballabh Tiwari Vs. Nagar Palika, Bhowali and others).
This Court is not agreeing with the principles laid down there to be
extracted to be applied in the present case because it was the case
where the proceedings were held under the Civil Laws and the
application moved therein which was considered was under Order 9
Rule 9 of CPC for of an order, dismissing the matter for non-prosecution. It is not the case here of dismissing the suit for want of
prosecution but rather due to the counsel's choice of not to
participate in the proceedings, despite of the notice having been
served upon him, having not appeared and that too when the next
date fixed was in his presence. The issue in the said judgement was
pertaining to the restoration of civil proceedings to its original
number, which was dismissed for want of prosecution; will not apply
in the present case.
41. Lastly, the learned counsel for the petitioner has referred and
relied on a judgement as reported in 2005 (2) LBESR 352, Laxmi
Palace (Cinema) through its Partner Sri Mukund Lal Vs.
Presiding Officer, Labor Court. The factual backdrop of the said
case was that when the petitioner of the said writ petition; had not
appeared after the due acceptance of the notice issued by the Court,
that was by way of his choice. The circumstances envisaged therein
are entirely different and distinct to the present one. Thus, this Court
is not in agreement with the principles as laid down in para 10 of the
said judgement, which is factually and circumstantially entirely
different to the present case in view of the findings and reasoning
which has been assigned by the labour Court by rendering the
impugned judgement under challenge here in the present writ
petition.
"10. Reverting to the case in hand, it is luculent from a
bare perusal that the award consists of four paragraphs.
The first paragraph contains details of parties and
dispute referred to it. The second and third paragraphs
deal with the dates fixed in the case in labour court. The
fourth and last paragraph contains conclusion. The

17
decisions discussed above, do point to the requirements
of taking into consideration the statements filed by the
party and it is only on comparative merits of claims and
counter claims that an exparte award has to be passed
and any exparte award filed without discussing the
claim and counter claims of the parties would not be
valid. In the instant case, the Labour Court merely laid
out factual aspects and jumped to the conclusion that
the workman was illegally terminated and was liable to
be reinstated in service. The requirement of law
envisaged for quasi judicial authority such as tribunal is
that the approach should be one simulating the judicial
standard and it must receive and place on record all the
necessary, relevant, cogent and acceptable material facts
germane and relevant to the facts in issue and inference
to form conclusion has to be drawn in conformity with
the judicial norms. In substance, the approach of the
Labour Court should be judicious. It transpires from a
perusal of the award that the Labour Court has not
discussed the materials on record nor it tried to discuss
the question for inference how the termination order
was illegal on the basis of materials on record. The least
that was expected of labour court was to discuss the
claims of the workman simulating the judicial standard
in case it was constrained to proceed exparte in the facts
and circumstances of the case i.e. to have analytically
examined the merit of the claims and recorded his
satisfaction with reference to the provisions of
the Industrial Disputes Act. It is well enunciated by
catena of decisions that the decision on merit must have
its genesis on material facts on record and the authority
is not permitted to traverse beyond the facts on record to
draw inference and make out a case of subjective
satisfaction for his conclusions. What operated in the
mind of the authority remained entombed and there is
no discussion to articulate the view that the workman
was illegally fired away and was entitled to
reinstatement. It is therefore explicit from the award
that the award was rendered without application of mind
and it cannot be given the complexion of an award on
merit. The award being bereft of any discussion on
merit even of claims of the workman thus, non-application of mind is conspicuously discernible in the
order."
42. While on the contrary, the learned counsel for the respondent
too has placed reliance upon some of the authorities of the Court, for
example, that as reported in 2010 AIR (Kar) (R) 729, J. Lokesh Vs.
Juggath Pharma Industries Limited, Bangalore, which in its para
4 has dealt with the situation that when the labour court has given a
fair and reasonable opportunity to the party to the proceedings of

18
reference, to appear and to contest the proceedings and the party
himself/herself, has chosen not to contest the same, as would be
reflected from the records of the present writ petition also, then in
that eventuality the petitioner himself has to be blamed, if the Court
has decided the matter against him, because the Courts are not
otherwise liable and responsible to issue consistent notices, in case if
there is deliberate absence by the petitioner in participating in the
proceedings. The relevant para is quoted hereunder:-
"4. The allegation that fair and reasonable opportunity
was not extended to the petitioner is far from truth and
cannot be countenanced. The order sheet dated 23-1-
2009 Annexure-E of the Labour Court discloses that
notice through RPAD when served on the petitioner,
informing the date of hearing, the petitioner was absent
though, the case was called thrice. The order in respect
of further dates of hearing also discloses that the
petitioner was absent. In the admitted fact that the
petitioner did not appear before the Labour Court on all
the dates of hearing, it is too far-fetched to contend that
the Labour Court ought to have issued yet another
notice to the petitioner to secure his presence in the
proceedings."
43. An identical view has been expressed in a judgement reported
in 2016 (1) LLJ 469 by Hon'ble Punjab and Haryana High Court
in the matters of Vinod Kumar Vs. Presiding Officer and others,
particularly, reference has been made to para 3, of the said
judgement which is quoted hereunder:-
"3. In the impugned award, the Court noticed that in the
written statement filed by the management contesting
the case their stand their was no relationship of
employer and employee between the parties. When the
workman went ex parte they took the stand that they did
not wish to lead evidence and rightly so. The facts
asserted by the management in its defence need not
have been established on record by evidence in view of
the uncontested proceedings leading to the award. Their
written statement was sufficient to non-suit the
workman if he had failed to discharge his burden of
proof. The Industrial Disputes (Central) Rules, 1957
empower Labour Courts and Tribunals to proceed ex
parte against defaulting party in absence of appearance
or proper explanation of non-appearance and therefore,
the Labour Court is within its jurisdiction to proceed ex
parte and to pass an ex parte award and while drawing
the award it could only deal with the available materials

19
on record, that is pleadings, evidence if any etc. to form
a view. The labour court has not believed the story
explaining reason for default of appearance and non-prosecution. If the labour court has not placed faith and
trust on unsubstantiated facts the it is not for this court
to sit in appeal and substitute its opinion for that of the
court below. Besides, the labour court has gone into the
conduct of the workman in delaying the proceedings
inordinately and without reasonable cause by failing
even to start his evidence for about four years. For this
there is no explanation even in the writ petition.
Moreover, the termination of service was effected 18
years ago in the year 1997 and the dispute was referred
in 2003, after six years which is also unreasonable
period and is without any explanation although no
period of limitation is prescribed in Section 10 (1) (c) of
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 but all the same delay
and laches should not be unreasonable. No manifest
injustice has resulted by the impugned award. On the
other hand manifest injustice will occasion on the
management if it is disturbed by uncalled for
interference in a stale claim and the fault lying squarely
on the workman not to have tended his stock by being
vigilant. It is worth noticing that the award and the
order impugned passed in 2008 and 2009 have been
challenged in the year 2012 which is also rather late and
all the stages of delay add up to enormous delay for any
effective legal redress of the grouse. For these reasons, I
find no cogent or valid ground to interfere either in the
award or the order declining to set aside the ex parte
award. The petition is, therefore, dismissed for lack of
substance and with no order as to costs."
44. Though it was the matter pertaining to the proceedings
emanating under the Industrial Disputes Central Rules of 1957, but
still the said judgement it has been held there that the labour court
had to proceed on the basis of evidence and the facts which were
brought on record before it and the aspects pertaining to the labour
court venturing into the act of workman in delaying the proceedings
without reasonable cause by not diligently participating in the court
proceedings, there it has been held, that in that eventuality, the
workman himself has to shoulder the burden of absence, without
there being a reasonable explanation given for the absence. In the
said judgement, the labour court has interpreted the impact of Rule
16(2) of the UP Industrial Dispute Rules, which uses the words
'sufficient cause', and has held that in case if there is failure on part
of an employee himself in failing to appear in the proceedings before

20
the labour Court, without there being sufficient cause at his behest or
at the behest of his counsel, no error could be held as against the
judgement rendered by labour Courts in the absence of the counsel.
45. The learned Senior Counsel for the respondent has relied upon
a judgement reported in 2003 (2) UPLBEC 1119, Suresh Chandra
Sharma Vs. The Presiding Officer, Labour Court-IVth UP,
where too the coordinate Bench of Allahabad High Court in its
finding recorded in para 10 and 11 of the said judgement, while
considering the argument of the workmen for justifying the reasons
for absence on the date fixed for hearing of the proceedings before
the labour court, the coordinate Bench in its para 10 and 11; had laid
down that once the labour Court has proceeded to adjudicate upon a
reference made to it, hence in the absence of there being any
statutory provisions and when the recall application not being in
consonance to Rule 16 of the Rules, no review or recall could have
been made to the judgement rendered on merits by the labour Court.
Paras 10 and 11 of the said judgement show that the bona fide of the
absence and the distinction between the appearance of the counsel
and the authorized representative of the department would be
certainly not applied in those cases which is entailed under normal
judicial proceedings.
"10. Therefore, in view of the aforesaid settled legal
proposition, it can be summarised that in absence of any
statutory provision providing for review, entertaining an
application for review or under the garb of
clarification/modification/correction is not permissible.
11. Learned counsel for the petitioner has submitted that
once the labour court has passed the Award, it becomes
functus officio and does not have the power to entertain
any application. Such an argument is admissible only in
case where the order passed by statutory authority is to
be reviewed and there is no statutory provision
prescribing for review as held by the Hon'ble Supreme
Court in Dr. Smt. Kuntesh Gupta v. Management of
Hindu Kanya Mahautdyalaya, Sitapur,:
1987(32)ELT8(SC), the Hon'ble Supreme Court held as
under :
"It is now established that a quasi-Judicial
authority cannot review its own order, unless the
power of review is expressly conferred on it by

21
the statute under which it derives its jurisdiction.
In the circumstances, it must be held that Vice-Chancellor acted wholly without
jurisdiction.........The said order of the Vice-Chancellor dated March 7, 1987 was a nullity."
46. The Allahabad High Court in its judgement reported in 1983
(1) LLJ 489, Sheo Sampat Lal Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, had
laid down the wider principles in para 7 of the said judgement, as to
under what circumstances, the latitude of the absence of the
representatives of either of the parties in the proceedings before the
labour Court could be ignored and once the surrounding
circumstances and evidence establishes that the absence was
deliberate and intentional established by conduct of the party, no
relaxation as such for the absence to be granted for the purpose of
recalling the order.
"7. It was next urged on behalf of the petitioner that
under the provisions of Clauses l8(a) and 22 read with
Clause 24 of the Standing Orders of the Company, it
was only the Manager or the Local Management alone
who could dismiss the petitioner. However, the order of
dismissal was passed by the General Works Manager,
Calcutta, who had no authority to pass that order. The
appointing authority was no doubt the Work's Manager,
Lucknow, but he did not pass the order of dismissal on
the ground that he had himself appeared as a witness in
the domestic enquiry against Sampat Lal. He, therefore,
referred the enquiry report to the General Works
Manager, Calcutta, who is a superior authority, for
necessary orders. The Board of Directors of the Union
Carbide India Limited, of which the Eveready
Flashlight Company, Lucknow, is a Division,
authorised the General Works Manager by a resolution
to pass an appropriate order. In these circumstances, it
is difficult to accept the contention that the dismissal
order was passed by a person who had no authority to
do so. The requisite authority having been conferred on
him, he was fully competent to pass the said order."
47. After having heard learned counsel for the parties at length,
the learned counsel for the petitioner has confined his arguments
from the view point that though he admits the fact that he had not
participated in the proceedings both departmental and also before the
labour Court diligently before the court, but what he contends that

22
the reason for his absence was that his representative has not given
him the information for appearance on the specified fixed dates. This
fact was a fact pleaded in the recall application paper No. 47D; but in
the writ petition, there is no such ground taken by the petitioner that
he could not appear before the labour court on account of lack of
supply of information by his counsel. Hence, he cannot be permitted
to argue a factual plea, without specifically incorporating the same in
his pleadings for giving challenge to the impugned awards.
48. Even otherwise also this Court is of the view that once the
petitioner has given an authority to the counsel to appear and present
his case and who had participated in the proceedings according to his
own convenience, it will be treated that his absence would amount to
be the absence of the petitioner and at this ripe stage, he cannot
contend and take the liberty to argue that since his counsel has not
informed him about the date fixed, contrary to pleadings, his case is
that, he cannot be made to suffer on account of the mistake of the
counsel. This argument is further diluted in view of the persistent
conduct of the petitioner, which has already been discussed above at
the stage when the disciplinary proceeding was being taken against
him, wherein he has not diligently and actively participated in the
proceedings. His conduct in the proceedings before the labour court,
if it is to be considered in the light of his diligence in the disciplinary
proceedings, it could be said that the reason for non appearance,
which is now being burdened on the counsel is an afterthought,
hence not acceptable by this Court.
49. Owing to the aforesaid reasons, it cannot be said that the
award of punishment by the disciplinary proceeding was an ex parte
against him because it was a voluntarily decision of the petitioner
himself not to participate in the proceedings, despite of there being
knowledge of the dates fixed, hence he will have to hold himself
responsible for his absence in the proceedings. Consequently, after
having thoroughly scrutinised the impugned orders under challenge,
I do not find that the labour court had committed any apparent legal
or procedural mistake, as such in the proceedings to decide the

23
matter after closing an opportunity of the petitioner, of leading
evidence. Hence, these writ petitions lack merit and the same are
accordingly dismissed.
50. However, there would be no order as to costs.
51. The reasons would follow for the connected writ petition,
since the factual and legal aspects being the same.
(Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.)
